sites.name: Ditch Plains beach and glacial-till cliffs
sites.story: Ditch Plains is the Atlantic-facing surf beach off Ditch Plains Road / Deforest Road (town address 6 Deforest Road). It is a cobble-and-till headland beach, not a broad barrier dune: a rock-bottom reef makes a consistent East Coast surf break, and glacial-till cliffs rise immediately west at Rheinstein Park / Shadmoor. Town Councilman David Lys has said a former life-saving station here stood about 100 feet farther seaward than today’s shoreline. The McCaffray / Rheinstein estate (house 1928) sat on the bluff between the recreational beach and Shadmoor. By the early 1970s a portion of the house was dangling over the eroded bluff; East Hampton Town bought the property in November 1972 and later dedicated Rheinstein Park and Nature Preserve (1993). Residual underground works remained; chronic bluff retreat later unearthed the estate’s cinder-block septic system, which the Town Board authorized emergency crews to remove (July 2026). East of the town beach, Montauk Shores Condominiums (the oceanfront mobile-home park) holds a rock revetment. After Hurricane Sandy, an expanded wall built in April 2013 was investigated by NYSDEC for oversized stone and excess elevation; a consent order required the crest lowered (14 ft east to 10 ft west) and no seaward toe expansion. Town Coastal Assessment Resilience Plan language, cited by Concerned Citizens of Montauk, says the revetment is “likely worsening shoreline erosion along adjacent shorelines.” Surfers also note a once-prominent small jetty that has been disappearing. Sandy and the following winter stripped the bathing beach to rocky hardpan and buried concrete; the town left Ditch closed to swimming in summer 2013. December 2023–January 2024 storms again destroyed the remnant primary dune, flooded streets a couple of blocks inland, wrecked the parking lot, and tore a porch off at least one house. Ditch was left out of the Army Corps FIMP downtown fill. The town placed about 5,800 cubic yards of sand in June 2024, then built a FEMA-oriented engineered dune (permit July 2025; about 20,000 cubic yards along ~2,200 feet; reported 16-foot finished “emergency structure,” earlier described as a 20-foot design). The dune runs from just east of the dirt-lot parking area to a few hundred feet west of the Seaside Avenue lot; two waterfront owners withheld easements, so work stopped short of the jetty. Officials have called it a temporary “speed bump,” with strategic retreat still on the long-term agenda. The Ditch Witch food truck has been a beachside staple since 1993. Kirk Park is not at Ditch Plains: it is the village-adjacent ocean beach on South Emerson Avenue (see ocean_beaches).

timeline.title: Bluff-top estate built above Ditch Plains
timeline.text: Richard Webb built the house and windmill in 1928 for stockbroker Walter P. McCaffray. The property later passed to the Jesuits and then to Sidney Rheinstein. It sat on the till bluff between the town beach and today’s Shadmoor / Rheinstein Park.

timeline.title: House over the bluff; town buys the estate
timeline.text: By the early 1970s a portion of the house dangled over the eroded bluff. In November 1972 the Town Board bought the land (federal aid $270,000; purchase $360,000). The remainder of the house was removed; the windmill was moved and later burned (1977). The site became Rheinstein Park and Nature Preserve in 1993.

timeline.title: Post-Sandy hardpan, swim closure, Montauk Shores revetment fight
timeline.text: After Sandy and winter storms, Ditch was a rocky expanse with exposed concrete; the town kept it closed to swimmers in 2013. Montauk Shores’ April 2013 rock revetment (885 linear feet authorized) was found by DEC to use stones larger than permitted and to exceed elevation limits. A consent order required regrading and no seaward expansion of the stone toe. Public access toward Cavett’s Cove was reduced except at the lowest tides.

timeline.title: December 2023–January 2024 storms erase the primary dune
timeline.text: Three unnamed storms destroyed the remnant dune, eroded the beach to hardpan, sent floodwater and sand a couple of blocks north, wrecked the parking lot, and tore a porch off at least one house. Longtime surfers called it the worst beach condition in 60 years. FIMP sand went to downtown Montauk, not Ditch. The town placed about 5,800 cubic yards in June 2024 as phase one.

timeline.title: Town engineered dune completed; historic septic unearthed in the bluff
timeline.text: After a July 2025 DEC permit and homeowner easements, Bistrian Materials placed about 20,000 cubic yards along ~2,200 feet. The Town Board marked completion of the 16-foot emergency dune on 15 January 2026 (from east of the dirt lot to west of the Seaside Avenue lot). Two houses lacked easements, so the fill stopped short of the jetty. In July 2026 the board authorized $14,700 emergency removal of the old Rheinstein-estate septic protruding from the bluff.

timeline.title: June 2024: 5,800 cy recreational fill
timeline.text: After the 2023–24 winter left Ditch down to hardpan (FIMP sand went downtown, not here), the town placed about 5,800 cubic yards of DEC-approved white sand on the recreational beach starting 17 June 2024.

timeline.title: Engineered dune: 20,000 cy along ~2,200 ft; crest +16 ft NAVD
timeline.text: Bistrian placed about 20,000 cubic yards along ~2,200 feet (fall 2025). Town 2024 Ditch-dune figures: 2020 remnant 1,925 cy above MSL had fallen to 544 cy by February 2024; rebuilt maximum 20,000 cy, crest +16 ft NAVD. First winter (2025–26) scarred the new dune about 10–12 ft west of the west lot.

timeline.title: Rheinstein / McCaffray septic pulled from the bluff
timeline.text: The 1928 McCaffray house sat on this till bluff; the town bought the dangling estate in 1972. In August 2026 crews removed the long-defunct septic from the Rheinstein Preserve bluff ($14,700 emergency).

sites.name: Soundview Drive beach (Fort Pond Bay / Block Island Sound)
sites.waterbody: Fort Pond Bay / Block Island Sound
sites.story: Soundview Drive is on Montauk’s NORTH shore, west of the Lake Montauk Harbor jetties, facing Block Island Sound—not the Atlantic. The road-adjacent beach runs about a mile from the west jetty toward Culloden Point. Town environmental staff describe 180 Soundview Drive as the start of the Culloden Point headlands (higher coastal bluffs); immediately east, Coastal Erosion Overlay Zone 4 runs nearly a mile to the jetties and is lined with revetments and bulkheads. West of those four parcels, about 8,000 feet of Culloden shoreline is free of erosion-control structures. Local government and court records treat this reach as the downdrift side of the 1926 harbor jetties: an east-to-west littoral drift is interrupted at the inlet, Gin Beach (east) holds surplus sand, and Soundview (west) is scoured. The 2007 Local Waterfront Revitalization Program, approved by the New York Secretary of State, acknowledged “downdrift scouring” along Soundview Drive. The town wrote USACE as early as 1994 about “severe downdrift scouring caused by the Federal jetties” and later permitted but never built a 5,000–10,000 cubic yard truck-haul bypass from town-owned Gin Beach to Soundview. Houses sit close behind bulkheads. On 5 February 1998 a Block Island Sound northeaster opened a 20-foot breach in a seven-owner bulkhead and put a house in jeopardy; a town drainage pipe ran through the wall near the failure. The 26–27 December 2011 northeaster produced 27 emergency permits to repair bulkheads. Hurricane Sandy (2012) left at least one Soundview house dangling over an eroded beach, pounded bulkheads, and leveled dunes that had separated the sound from Gosman’s, damaging the road. Eleven Soundview / Captain Kidd’s Path owners sued the town, county, state, and United States (Cangemi). A 2018 jury awarded about $356,000 to seven owners; the district court then dismissed the case (2019) and the Second Circuit affirmed (2021): the town holds title under the jetties but USACE has exclusive federal-navigation control, and the town was not shown to have intended the 1942 handover to cause the western erosion. In 2024 the Town Board refused to move 180–192 Soundview Drive (763 linear feet) from Zone 2 (hardening restricted) into Zone 4. Counsel for one owner said Culloden Point had lost 150 feet in 20 years—an advocate figure, not a town measurement. The 2025–26 Lake Montauk deepening is designed to place dredged sand on the eroded shore immediately west of the west jetty, the first large federal bypass toward this beach.

timeline.title: Harbor jetties begin starving the mile of beach to the west
timeline.text: Private jetties at the new Lake Montauk inlet interrupted north-shore littoral drift. Town staff later wrote that the jetties “have always caused downdrift erosion,” later mapped as Zone 4 from the west jetty to Soundview Drive. Subsequent bulkheads and revetments became the reach’s main character.

timeline.title: February 5 northeaster breaches a Soundview bulkhead
timeline.text: Wind-driven Block Island Sound waves opened a 20-foot-wide hole in a bulkhead shared by seven Soundview Drive houses and put one house in jeopardy. Fill behind the wall “came tumbling out.” Residents had been asking the town and USACE to dredge the harbor and put sand on beaches east and west of the channel.

timeline.title: Town LWRP records downdrift scouring on Soundview
timeline.text: The final Local Waterfront Revitalization Program, approved by the New York Secretary of State in 2007, stated that the jetties caused downdrift scouring to beaches along Soundview Drive. That finding is recited in the Second Circuit’s Cangemi opinion.

timeline.title: December northeaster: 27 emergency bulkhead permits
timeline.text: The 26–27 December 2011 northeast storm was especially damaging. Residents sought 27 emergency permits to repair bulkheads and otherwise shore up Soundview property. The Cangemi federal suit followed.

timeline.title: Sandy undermines a Soundview house and overwashes near Gosman’s
timeline.text: Block Island Sound again hit Soundview and Culloden. A house owned by Janet Cole was left dangling over a badly eroded beach. To the east, dunes between the sound and Gosman’s were leveled and the road damaged. At least one house was reported severely undermined and in danger of collapse.

timeline.title: Cangemi appeal fails; town not liable for jetty downdrift
timeline.text: The Second Circuit (13 F.4th 115) affirmed dismissal. Plaintiffs had alleged the jetties caused the western scour. The court held USACE—not the town—controls the federal navigation project, and no trial evidence showed the town knew in 1942 that handing over the jetties would erode the private beaches to the west.

timeline.title: Sandy: rocks on Soundview Drive; house undermined
timeline.text: Block Island Sound threw former shore-protection rocks onto Soundview Drive pavement and undermined at least one house. North shore — not the Atlantic.

timeline.title: 184 Soundview: more than 24 ft of bluff lost
timeline.text: At a 9 July 2024 Town Board session, counsel said the Iudicones at 184 Soundview Drive had lost more than 24 feet of bluff that year. Zone 4 runs from the west harbor jetty to just east of 180 Soundview.

timeline.title: 16 May 2024: Culloden Point lawn on an eroding precipice
timeline.text: The East Hampton Star photographed a lawn dripping off an eroding precipice at Culloden Point; the shoreline to the east is almost completely hardened.

sites.name: Montauk Harbor / Lake Montauk inlet jetties (Star Island)
sites.facing: north (inlet opens to Block Island Sound)
sites.story: Lake Montauk (historically Great Pond / Lake Wyandanch) was Long Island’s largest freshwater lake until Carl Fisher’s Montauk Beach Development Corporation cut it through to Block Island Sound. A 1926 attempt closed in an easterly storm; the final cut was in 1927. Blueprints called for a yacht channel about 250 feet wide and 15 feet deep, with jetties set 60 feet into the ground. A Corps jetty history table records private construction in 1926: east jetty 750 feet, west jetty 981 feet, 1- to 4-ton stone. Star Island, just inside the inlet, was connected to the mainland by a causeway and became the yacht-club / casino / later Coast Guard station node. In 1941 Fisher’s company deeded the jetties and lakebed to the Town of East Hampton. In 1942 the town granted the United States a permanent easement for a Federal Navigation Project; the Navy funded a 231-foot shoreward extension of the west jetty. Congress authorized the FNP in the Rivers and Harbors Act of 1945: a channel 12 feet deep (MLLW/MLW sources vary in wording) and 150 feet wide for about 0.7 miles from Block Island Sound to the yacht basin east of Star Island; a boat basin 10 feet deep, 400 by 900 feet, northwest of Star Island; both jetties; and sport-fishing walkways on the jetties. Federal development of the structures was completed in 1968 when the jetties were repaired and the east jetty extended 350 feet (about 18,400 tons of stone). USACE repaired the east jetty in 1995 and dredged periodically from 1966 to 2011. The town still holds title; USACE maintains the jetties. The jetties fix the inlet and trap the local east-to-west sand stream. Updrift Gin Beach (east) accretes; downdrift Soundview (west) erodes. Shoaling in the channel is the navigation twin of that interruption. A 1995 Corps reconnaissance study recommended rehabilitating the jetties, deepening the entrance, and using dredged and bypassed sand on the western shore. The town later approved a 5,000–10,000 cy Gin Beach-to-Soundview truck bypass and obtained permits but never started it. A 2014 Corps public meeting offered a no-action plan, a ~$26 million navigation-only deepening with west-shore placement and a five-year cycle, and a ~$41 million navigation-plus-storm-risk plan that added about 230,000 cubic yards of bypass and regular bypassing. A Project Partnership Agreement for a Section 107 deepening was executed in September 2022. The constructed plan deepens the channel to −17 ft MLLW, creates a 100-foot-wide deposition basin immediately east of the channel, and places sandy dredged material on the eroded shoreline west of the west jetty (project descriptions cite about 110,000 cubic yards to the downdrift beach; rock goes to a New York offshore reef). USACE awarded an $8.9 million contract to H&L Contracting on 18 September 2025; dredging began that fall with a scheduled finish of 31 January 2026. That placement is the first large federal inlet-bypass toward Soundview.

timeline.title: Private jetties built; first cut closes in a storm
timeline.text: Private interests built east (750 ft) and west (981 ft) jetties at the lake entrance. Fisher workmen cut a ditch to Block Island Sound in 1925–26, but an easterly storm closed it (County Review, March 1926). Jetties were designed 60 feet into the ground to hold a yacht channel.

timeline.title: Final cut opens Lake Montauk as a salt harbor
timeline.text: J.W. Hennessey Corporation completed the channel connecting Great Pond to Block Island Sound. Fisher renamed the waterbody Lake Montauk. The new inlet became home to New York’s largest commercial and sportfishing fleets and shifted the port from shallow, rocky Fort Pond Bay.

timeline.title: Federal Navigation Project authorized; 1942 Navy/US easement already in place
timeline.text: The town took title in 1941 and granted a permanent federal easement in 1942; the Navy paid for a 231-foot shoreward extension of the west jetty. The Rivers and Harbors Act of 1945 (Pub. L. 79-14) authorized the 12-foot, 150-foot-wide channel to the Star Island yacht basin, the 10-foot northwest boat basin, and both jetties.

timeline.title: Jetties repaired; east jetty extended 350 feet
timeline.text: After a 1967 survey found poor condition, the jetties were repaired and the east jetty lengthened 350 feet using about 18,400 tons of stone. Federal development of the harbor structures is treated as complete as of 1968. The east jetty was repaired again in 1995.

timeline.title: Reconnaissance study recommends west-shore bypass
timeline.text: USACE’s Lake Montauk Harbor Reconnaissance Study found navigation impaired by east-jetty deterioration and recommended jetty rehab, channel deepening, and use of dredged/bypassed sand on the eroded western shoreline. A town Gin Beach-to-Soundview bypass of 5,000–10,000 cy was later permitted but never built.

timeline.title: Channel deepening to −17 ft MLLW; sand to the west jetty beach
timeline.text: After a 2022 PPA with East Hampton, USACE awarded H&L Contracting $8.9 million on 18 September 2025 to deepen the channel from −12 to −17 ft MLLW, maintain an east-side deposition basin, place about 110,000 cubic yards of sand on the downdrift shore west of the west jetty, and send rock to a state reef. Work was scheduled through 31 January 2026.

timeline.title: Emergency 10,500 cy west of west jetty; ~150,000 cy toward Mermaid Beach
timeline.text: February 2025 emergency dredge placed 10,500 cy on the beach immediately west of the inlet. The full deepening targeted about 150,000 cy to Mermaid Beach (west of the west jetty). NORTH shore feeder — not downtown FIMP.

timeline.title: Nearly 90,000 cy gone; Sunset Beach feeder then ~12 ft blizzard cut
timeline.text: By 15 January 2026 the Town Board was told nearly 90,000 cy had been removed from the Lake Montauk dredge. Inlet-floor sand piled on Sunset Beach west of the jetty totaled 95,000-plus cy; a March 2026 blizzard cut the new feeder beach about 12 feet. NORTH harbor.

sites.name: South-shore ocean beaches (downtown to the Ditch approach)
sites.story: This site is the Atlantic strand on the SOUTH side of the hamlet—the developed ocean beach from the Benson Reservation / Umbrella Beach (South Eton Street) through Kirk Park (South Emerson Avenue, next to the IGA) and motel row to just east of Surfside Place / Atlantic Terrace, then the open strand toward Ditch Plains. It is not Soundview and not the lighthouse ocean bluffs. After the 1938 hurricane flooded Napeague and briefly made Montauk an island, the business district was later re-established immediately next to this ocean beach, so commercial buildings sit one dune from the Atlantic. The beach is a typical south-shore dissipative strand: storms cut scarps, push sand into offshore bars, and—on this coast—surveys show the visible beach often rebuilds within about a month if sand has not left the system (Tanski 2012). Downtown is also a long-term erosion/hot-spot reach in the FIMP “headland” compartment. Hurricane Sandy (29 October 2012) removed the pre-storm berm and severely scarped the dunes, leaving motel-row foundations exposed from the Royal Atlantic west toward Ocean Surf / Ocean End; Gurney’s Beach Club and boardwalk were destroyed. As a Sandy interim, USACE and New York placed sand-filled geotextile bags along about 3,100 feet of dune from South Emery Street to the Atlantic Terrace motel (construction October 2015–April 2016). Buried bags were meant as a one-time stabilizer until a sand-only plan; locals nicknamed the result “Dirtbag Beach.” Annual sand cover was shared among Corps, State, Town, and County. Winter 2023–24 storms stripped that cover and exposed the 2015 geocubes/geobags. FIMP’s downtown component is sand-only sediment management: a berm about 60 feet wide at +9.5 ft NGVD29, designed as a feeder beach that works with the 2016 geotextile core. Plans called for about 450,000 cubic yards along approximately 6,000 feet from the Benson Reservation to just east of Surfside Place, widening the construction template on the order of 475 feet above and below sea level, then 400,000–450,000 cubic yards every four years for 30 years. Great Lakes Dredge & Dock’s hopper Ellis Island pumped from an offshore borrow area (described as off Napeague / about 2,000 feet offshore). Placement began 6 February 2024 and finished in about 20 days; town and press totals were about 462,000–475,000 cubic yards; a later Corps news release said 500,000 cubic yards along 4,100 feet at about $11.7 million, 100 percent federal under the Sandy appropriations act. Sand fencing, beach grass, and rebuilt walkovers followed. Damaged wooden dune crossovers were later removed and replaced with sand paths. Ditch Plains was not included.

timeline.title: Hurricane of 1938 overwashes Napeague; downtown later sits on the ocean
timeline.text: The 1938 hurricane flooded across Napeague, turning Montauk into an island (the isthmus was not again flooded to that extent until Sandy). Floodwaters inundated the then-main downtown; the business district was subsequently established about three miles south, immediately next to the Atlantic beach that FIMP now nourishes.

timeline.title: Sandy strips the downtown berm and scars the dunes
timeline.text: The wide pre-storm berm was effectively removed and dunes were scarped. Motel-row foundations were exposed; Gurney’s Beach Club restaurant, Beach Barge, and boardwalk were destroyed. Trucks of sand were rolled in immediately. Town FIMP materials treat this as the event that forced an interim stabilizer ahead of reformulation.

timeline.title: Geotextile-bag dune completed (South Emery to Atlantic Terrace)
timeline.text: A November 2014 Corps study recommended sand-filled geotextile bags along about 3,100 feet of dune. The Town–USACE–NYSDEC PPA was signed in February 2015; construction ran October 2015–April 2016. Bags were buried under sand as a one-time commercial-district stabilizer. The beach was nicknamed “Dirtbag Beach.”

timeline.title: Feb 2024 FIMP: 450,000 cy / 6,000 ft / 20 days
timeline.text: Ellis Island pumped the downtown Atlantic beach (South Eton Street to Surfside Place / Kirk Park). Official fill 450,000 cubic yards along 6,000 feet; work finished in 20 days (~6–25 Feb 2024). Town/press totals later 462,000–475,000 cy. Ditch was not included.

timeline.title: Post-storm scarps and recovery (south-shore process)
timeline.text: Sea Grant’s south-shore primer documents that even modest storms cut visible scarps, that most sand removed above the waterline often remains in the beach system, and that surveyed south-shore beaches usually rebuild within about a month. Downtown’s 2023–24 scarps that exposed the 2015 bags are the local instance of that process on a nourished, geotextile-cored dune.

timeline.title: Gurney’s Inn beach food-service building lost to Sandy
timeline.text: A food-service building on the beach at Gurney’s Inn was lost to Hurricane Sandy’s 29 October 2012 assault. SOUTH / Atlantic motel row — not Soundview.

timeline.title: October 2015: about 20 ft of dry sand left before geotextile
timeline.text: Just before the Army Corps sandbag dune, people walked a narrow strip of dry sand on downtown Montauk’s ocean beach — about 20 feet of dry sand left at the motel-row toe.

sites.name: Montauk Point Lighthouse, Turtle Cove, and Camp Hero bluffs
sites.facing: east and south (Turtle Hill cliffs fall to the Atlantic on the east and south; Turtle Cove is the south-side embayment)
sites.story: The octagonal sandstone lighthouse stands on Turtle Hill at 41.07099°N, 71.85709°W, the eastern tip of Long Island. Construction ran 7 June–5 November 1796 (authorized 1792 under Washington; first lit 1797). It was placed at the west end of the Turtle Hill plateau about 300 feet from the bluff because agents already noted that “Montauk Point is washed by the sea in storms” and “wastes very fast” (NY Natural Heritage Program, quoting period siting notes). The tower has not been moved. The National Park Service historic-light inventory states “Has tower been moved? NO.” What happened in 1996 was a transfer of ownership: on 30 September 1996 President Clinton signed legislation conveying the property to the Montauk Historical Society (the Society had leased it since 1987). A 1996 wood bandstand was built for the bicentennial; Giorgina Reid was honored that year for terracing work. Relocation was later evaluated by USACE as an alternative (surfers in 2006 analogized to Cape Hatteras, which was moved 2,900 feet in 1999) and rejected as more costly, damaging to the historic setting, and risky on the two-hill terrain. The commonly cited “~290 ft inland move in 1996” is not supported by these records; 290–300 feet is the original setback from the cliff, not a relocation distance. Distance-to-bluff figures in published sources: original ~300 feet (1796); about 200 feet of ocean-facing bluff recession since 1797 (National Historic Landmark nomination); about 75 feet remaining in 1998 (New York Times); “less than 100 feet” in USACE project descriptions and the 2023 East Hampton Star; an older Corps fact sheet still says “less than 50 feet of land in front of the structure.” After the 2021–23 revetment the published buffer remains on the order of less than 100 feet of bluff, with armor at the toe. Armor history: a 1944 storm dropped about 12 feet of cliff; in 1945 USACE built an ~840-foot stone seawall that 1950s storms overtopped and collapsed. The Coast Guard in 1967–69 considered replacing the tower with a steel light farther from the edge; public protest stopped demolition. Giorgina Reid began reed-trench terracing on Earth Day 1970 and worked through 1986; a Coast Guard gabion was added in 1972. Hurricane Bob and the 1991 “Perfect Storm” wrecked much of that work. A ~770-foot / ~28,000-ton seawall, built with Corps consultation, was completed about 1997; the Historical Society and State also added rock in 1992–97. The NHL nomination describes a ca. 1945 revetment rebuilt in the 1990s as two tiers of boulders rising about 20 feet. USACE’s 2005–06 feasibility study recommended a new stone revetment rather than relocation, breakwaters, T-groins, or nourishment. After Sandy, a 2017 Limited Re-evaluation and 2019 PPA (65% federal / 35% state) led to construction March 2021–June 2023: about 1,000 linear feet rebuilt, existing 5- and 10-ton stone reused, new 10–20-ton armor, terracing and vegetation above the crest, more than 60,000 tons of granite. The wall was nearly doubled in width, Turtle Cove was cut about in half, and two benches were formed for foot traffic across the face. Total project cost is reported at $44 million. Camp Hero State Park (41.0706°N, 71.8710°W), immediately west, has 75- to 80-foot Atlantic bluffs at Turtle Cove that park and Surfrider comments treat as still actively eroding and unsafe at the edge; swimming is not permitted in the park.

timeline.title: Tower completed ~300 feet from the Turtle Hill bluff
timeline.text: John McComb Jr. finished the lighthouse on 5 November 1796 on a 71-foot headland. Period siting notes already called Montauk Point a rapidly wasting shore. The ocean-facing bluff has since receded on the order of 200 feet (NHL nomination).

timeline.title: First Corps seawall after a 1944 cliff collapse
timeline.text: A 1944 storm dropped about 12 feet of cliff. In 1945 USACE placed an ~840-foot stone seawall at the toe. Early-1950s storms and hurricanes washed over it and collapsed it. Erosion continued; the Coast Guard later considered a steel replacement tower (announced around 1969 for 1972).

timeline.title: Giorgina Reid starts reed-trench terracing
timeline.text: On Earth Day 1970 Reid began unpaid terracing of the Turtle Hill cliffs. The Coast Guard added a gabion in 1972. She stabilized the eastern cliff by 1985 and retired in 1986 (Reagan commendation). Hurricane Bob and the 1991 Halloween storm destroyed much of the work and triggered a new federal study.

timeline.title: Ownership transfer — not a 290-foot move
timeline.text: On 30 September 1996 the lighthouse property was conveyed to the Montauk Historical Society. The NPS light-station inventory records the tower as unmoved. USACE later studied relocation and rejected it. The ~290–300 foot figure in circulation matches the original bluff setback, not a 1996 inland move (Cape Hatteras, by contrast, was moved 2,900 feet in 1999). A 770-foot / ~28,000-ton seawall associated with that era was completed about 1997; the Times then put the remaining cliff buffer at about 75 feet.

timeline.title: Corps chooses revetment over moving the light
timeline.text: The October 2005 / March 2006 feasibility study recommended a new stone revetment. Alternatives included no-action, relocation, offshore breakwater with beach, T-groins with beach, and nourishment. Surfers opposed a larger wall as a threat to the Turtle Cove break and proposed a Hatteras-style move; the Corps kept the in-place revetment.

timeline.title: 1,000-foot granite revetment finished; Turtle Cove narrowed
timeline.text: H&L Contracting rebuilt ~1,000 linear feet (stone work December 2022; site restoration June 2023). More than 60,000 tons of granite nearly doubled the wall; Turtle Cove was cut about in half; two pedestrian benches were built on a new seaward bulge. Published remaining bluff buffer: less than 100 feet (USACE / Star 2023), with the new armor at the toe. Camp Hero’s Turtle Cove bluffs immediately west remain steep, fragile, and closed to swimming.
